messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 29, Arjun Patel came to treatment after years of insisting to himself that what happened was behind him. He had been a child when his family fled political violence and spent months moving through temporary shelters and transit camps before reaching the United States. What stays with him most vividly is not a single image but the bodily atmosphere of that time: being pressed shoulder to shoulder with strangers in overcrowded rooms, the sense that there was no way out, men moving too close without warning, and the sour smell of alcohol on adults whose moods felt dangerous and unreadable. Certain places still carry an immediate charge for him—narrow waiting areas, packed subway platforms, building lobbies where people bunch together near an elevator. The smell of alcohol can make his chest seize before he has even located where it is coming from, and when someone unfamiliar steps toward him in a crowded space, his body surges into alarm before he has had time to tell himself he is in present-day Boston and not trapped somewhere else.

As he got older, Arjun came to organize these reactions around a set of painful conclusions about himself and other people. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that danger hid behind ordinary faces and ordinary gestures. He was also certain that something about him was visible, as if other people could look at him and immediately know what had happened to him, know he came from that history, know there was something wrong with him. Those beliefs sharpened the force of particular triggers. Crowded spaces did not feel neutral and overstimulating in a general way; they felt full of strangers he could not trust. Physical locations that resembled transit halls or institutional corridors drew his attention because they seemed to expose him, and the smell of alcohol did not register as incidental because in his mind it belonged to people who could turn unpredictable at any moment.

He now works as an architect, a profession he chose in part because structure, space, and control feel deeply important to him. Even there, the symptoms have woven themselves into his daily life. Site visits are especially difficult. If a contractor or client he does not know well approaches him in a tight stairwell or on a noisy construction floor, he feels the threat instantly in his body: muscles tensing, heart racing, a jolt of readiness before thought catches up. The reaction itself leaves him humiliated. When he notices himself scanning exits or recoiling from an ordinary approach, it seems to confirm his private conviction that there is something defective about him, that he is not like other people and cannot inhabit the world normally. And the more threatened he feels by strangers in routine settings, the more certain he becomes that safety cannot be trusted just because someone else says it is there.

Over time he developed ways of managing this that initially felt sensible. Because he believed others were untrustworthy and that his damage was somehow visible, he began trying to keep absolute control over whatever he could. He restricts his eating rigidly, describing it less as concern about weight than as the one area where he can impose order and not feel at the mercy of his body. He works hard to suppress any thought related to the past, cutting himself off internally the moment an image or sensation starts to emerge. He keeps his mind occupied almost constantly with drawings, podcasts, work problems, or phone games, because silence feels too risky. Yet these habits have had their own effects. Going long hours without eating leaves him more physically keyed up, and in that depleted state sudden closeness, noise, or the smell of alcohol can feel even more immediately dangerous. His constant mental effort to push things away has also deepened his sense that there must be something profoundly wrong with him if his mind has to be managed so tightly all the time.

In recent months the cycle has tightened. The more threatened he feels in ordinary public encounters, the more he notices the very settings he dreads: train platforms, office receptions, crowded design reviews, bars near project sites where coworkers gather after meetings. He has started declining team events if they are held in busy restaurants, partly because of the crowding and partly because the smell of beer or liquor hits him so fast. Colleagues experience him as private and hard to read, which fits too easily with his belief that distance is safer. Being alone has not brought relief. If anything, the endless effort to distract himself and keep control has left him more convinced that other people would see him as damaged if they got too close, and less able to believe reassurance when friends tell him he is safe now.

What finally brought him in was an incident at work: during a packed elevator ride to a client presentation, a stranger shifted suddenly beside him and he felt a wave of terror so immediate that he had to get off on the wrong floor and sit on the ground until the shaking eased. Afterward he could not stop thinking that his body had betrayed him in public and that everyone must have seen it. He is seeking help because he is exhausted by the vigilance and by how small his life has become. What frightens him most is the possibility that this is permanent—that he will never trust anyone, never feel safe in his own body, and never enter an ordinary crowded room without bracing for danger.
